papers.title: Exploring the Potential of Ultra-Low-Bit Inference on LLM Accelerators
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27561v1

summary.one_liner: The paper proposes VQACC, a modest change to a systolic-array LLM accelerator's operand buffer access logic and data mapping so that vector-quantized weight codebook lookups reuse existing storage and ports, reporting a 2.63x speedup over the EVA baseline at 0.17% extra compute-array area.
summary.plain: Large language models are very big, and one way to shrink them is to store their numbers as short codes that point into a small lookup table, called a codebook. Turning those codes back into usable numbers requires many lookups, which clash with how existing AI chips move data, so past fixes added special-purpose hardware. This paper argues that today's chips already have the spare memory and access ports needed, and that the way they are wired just needs rethinking; the authors report that their version runs about 2.63 times faster than a prior baseline (EVA) while adding very little chip area.
summary.why: Running large models on cheaper, lower-power hardware is a practical concern for deploying AI, and this shows a way to get the benefit of extreme compression without building a separate accelerator. The claims come only from the abstract; the workloads, measurement setup, and comparison details are not given here, so the size of the gain should be read with that in mind.
summary.background:
- Quantization: storing model numbers with fewer bits to save memory and time.
- Vector quantization (VQ): grouping several values and replacing them with one index into a shared codebook.
- Codebook lookup: fetching the stored values that an index points to, then using them in computation.
- Systolic array: a grid of simple processing units that passes data across neighbors, common in AI accelerators.
- Operand buffer: on-chip memory that holds the inputs fed to the compute array; its ports limit how fast data can be read.
- Dataflow: the order and route by which data moves through hardware.
- Dequantization: converting compressed codes back into full values before computing with them.
- EVA: the prior accelerator design used as the comparison point in the paper.

papers.abstract: Vector quantization (VQ) enables ultra-low-bit compression of large language models (LLMs) by encoding groups of values as compact codebook indexes. However, reconstructing these values for computation requires frequent codebook lookups, which conflict with the dataflows of conventional LLM accelerators and limit the performance gains from VQ compression. Consequently, prior work has resorted to VQ-specific accelerator designs, which either incur substantial additional hardware overhead or support only a limited range of inference scenarios. In this work, we argue that existing systolic-array-based LLM accelerators already possess the essential hardware resources for efficient VQ inference, but lack the mechanisms to effectively exploit them. To bridge this gap, we present VQACC, an architectural enhancement that jointly redesigns the existing operand buffer's access logic and data mapping to reuse its storage and port resources for codebook lookups, seamlessly integrating dequantization into the normal operand-addressing dataflow. Evaluation shows that VQACC achieves a 2.63$\times$ speedup over the EVA baseline, with additional hardware occupying only 0.17\% of the compute array's area.

papers.title: Acceleration of Sparse and Irregular Workloads through Energy-Efficient Stream Extensions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26939v1

summary.one_liner: A thesis proposing a core-coupled hardware stream extension for RISC-V processors that accelerates sparse and irregular workloads (affine and indirect streams, sparse tensor intersection and union), evaluated in a 432-core 2.5D system in 12nm FinFET and extended to chip-level interconnects.
summary.plain: Modern chips are built to run orderly, predictable computations well, but many real tasks involve scattered, unpredictable data access, so the chip's calculating units sit idle most of the time (the text cites under 10% utilization). This thesis designs add-on hardware that fetches and feeds such scattered data streams to the processor so it stays busy, and reports tests on a large chip built from many small processors.
summary.why: Sparse and irregular workloads underlie sparse neural networks, physics simulations, and graph analytics, so efficiency gains here could matter for those fields. The text reports benchmark results on its own prototype, but it does not show how these gains would carry over to commercial systems, so that remains open.
summary.background:
- Hardware "stream" units: separate helpers that fetch data from memory in a planned sequence while the main processor computes.
- Sparse data: arrays where most entries are zero, so only a few values need storing and processing.
- Functional unit utilization: the share of time a chip's arithmetic units are actually doing useful work.
- RISC-V: an open processor instruction set design.
- Stencil computation: updating each point in a grid using its neighbours, common in physics simulations.
- Dennard scaling and Moore's law: historical trends of faster, cheaper transistors that have slowed down.
- 2.5D integration: placing several chips side by side on a shared connecting base rather than stacking them.

papers.abstract: The slowdown of Moore's law and Dennard scaling has motivated computer architects to uphold performance scaling through architectural specialization. So far, most efforts have focused on highly regular workloads, which exhibit good data locality, ample reuse, and a data-independent execution flow. As this specialization hits diminishing returns, attention shifts towards sparse and irregular workloads, which are essential to applications like sparse neural networks, multiphysics simulations, and graph analytics. However, they lack the convenient properties of highly regular compute that modern architectures are optimized for, resulting in very low (<10%) functional unit utilization on traditional CPUs and GPUs. The most promising approaches to their general hardware acceleration leverage memory streams, which decouple data movement from execution. In this thesis, we explore energy-efficient hardware stream extensions that significantly accelerate sparse and irregular workloads in general-purpose systems without specializing to specific application domains or compromising on regular-workload performance. We design a flexible, core-coupled stream extension supporting affine and indirect streams as well as intersection and union of sparse tensors. We integrate it into an energy-efficient RISC-V compute cluster, achieving significant performance and energy efficiency benefits on general sparse linear algebra, and further use it to accelerate stencil computations, spiking neural network inference, and model-predictive control. We evaluate it at scale in a 432-core 2.5D RISC-V system fabricated in 12nm FinFET, achieving leading compute utilization and energy efficiency on sparse and irregular workloads while remaining competitive on regular workloads. Finally, we extend chip-level interconnects with end-to-end irregular streams, improving performance, energy efficiency, and bus utilization.

papers.title: Bring Cloud-Native Networking to FreeBSD Jails: Porting Calico from Linux
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27320v1

summary.background:
- Container: a way to run an isolated program with its own view of files and network, sharing the host's operating system.
- FreeBSD Jails: FreeBSD's built-in container-like isolation.
- CNI (Container Network Interface) plugin: a standard add-on that handles networking for containers in orchestration systems such as Kubernetes.
- Calico: a widely used networking plugin that also enforces rules about which containers may communicate.
- iptables / ipfw: packet-filtering rule systems on Linux and FreeBSD respectively.
- Netlink / routing sockets: the interfaces programs use to query and change network settings in the kernel.
- Network namespace / vnet: a way to give each container its own separate network stack.
summary.one_liner: The paper describes porting Calico, a widely used Kubernetes-style container networking plugin, to FreeBSD Jails by swapping Linux networking components for FreeBSD equivalents (ipfw for iptables, routing sockets for netlink, vnet for network namespaces).
summary.plain: Software that runs many isolated programs on one computer, called containers, needs a way to connect them to networks and set rules about who can talk to whom. On Linux, a popular tool called Calico does this, but FreeBSD (an operating system with its own style of containers called Jails) lacked an equivalent, so users set things up by hand. This paper describes adapting Calico to run on FreeBSD by replacing Linux-only pieces with FreeBSD's own built-in tools.
summary.why: It aims to let FreeBSD work with the same container orchestration systems that Linux users rely on, which could matter for anyone running FreeBSD servers at scale. The text is a short abstract only, so it does not report measured results, and how complete or well-tested the port is cannot be judged from it.

papers.abstract: While Linux containers benefit from a rich ecosystem of Container Network Interface (CNI) plugins such as Calico and Cilium, FreeBSD Jails lacked native, standardized solutions for advanced networking. As a result, users have relied on manual, error-prone configurations, limiting scalability and integration with modern orchestration platforms. This paper introduces porting Calico, a widely adopted CNI plugin, to the FreeBSD operating system. Our approach replaced Linux-specific components with FreeBSD-native equivalents: iptables with ipfw, netlink sockets with routing sockets, and Linux network namespaces with FreeBSD's vnet. This work aims to bridge the gap between Linux and BSD container networking. By providing scalable, policy-driven capabilities that are compatible with existing Linux-centric infrastructure, FreeBSD can participate more fully in the broader container networking ecosystem.

papers.title: Contention-Aware Flexible Execution for Machine Learning Workloads
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26840v1

summary.background:
- GPU (graphics processing unit): a chip with many parallel cores, widely used to train and run AI models.
- Kernel: a single compute job launched on a GPU, such as one matrix multiplication.
- Concurrent execution: running several kernels at once so the chip is used more fully.
- Contention: competition for shared resources like cache and memory bandwidth, which slows each job.
- Memory-bound vs. compute-bound: whether a job is limited by how fast data moves or by how fast arithmetic can be done.
- Training vs. inference (prefill and decode): training updates a model; inference uses it to generate output, with prefill and decode being its two phases.
- End-to-end speedup: the improvement in total run time for a whole workload, not just one piece.
summary.one_liner: A characterization of how concurrently running GPU kernels slow each other down on AMD MI300X hardware, followed by CAFEML, a contention-aware scheduler that tunes operator overlap and resource allocation for ML training and inference, reporting up to 13% end-to-end speedup without kernel rewrites.
summary.plain: Modern AI software runs many small computing tasks (called kernels) at the same time on a graphics processor, and they compete for shared parts of the chip such as memory and cache, so each can run slower. This paper measures how much that slowdown happens on a current datacenter AI chip, and sorts the results by whether a task is limited by memory or by computation, and whether it is large or small. It then proposes simple scheduling rules for when to start overlapping tasks and how to split chip resources between them.
summary.why: Keeping expensive AI accelerators busy is a practical concern for anyone running large models, and the paper suggests that the default "start whatever is ready first" policy used by frameworks leaves performance on the table. The gain reported (up to 13% end-to-end) comes from scheduling changes alone, which is a modest but practically relevant result; the text does not show how well it generalizes beyond the scenarios tested.

papers.abstract: Concurrent kernel execution is a ubiquitous paradigm in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) across both training and inference. That said, concurrency causes potential slowdown as concurrent kernels contend for limited GPU resources (cores, caches, memory bandwidth), which are shared between these kernels rather than exclusively available to one, as in isolated execution. This raises an important research question: to what extent does concurrency slow down kernel execution and how can it be mitigated. To answer this question, our work presents two studies. First, we characterize concurrent kernel execution extensively for the first time, to our knowledge. We conduct not just performance analysis of concurrent kernels but also memory behavior under concurrency on state-of-the-art AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs designed for datacenter AI, using the AMD-internal millisecond sampler. Based on the observations, we share insights on the slowdown along two dimensions (memory vs. compute bound, large vs. small kernels) to inform future optimizations. Second, we put the derived insights to use, aiming to deliver higher performance via targeted, flexible overlap of ML operators. Frameworks today make the simple decision of early-first for concurrent kernels, which is suboptimal. Noticing the opportunity that ML dataflow has inherent flexibility in which operators can be overlapped and how hardware resources can be allocated, we deduce simple heuristics to tune both overlap anchors and resource allocation for concurrent kernels to improve performance. We evaluate our proposed contention-aware flexible execution (termed CAFEML) across a variety of ML scenarios (inference decode, inference prefill, training) and demonstrate a speedup of up to 13% end-to-end with simple scheduling changes and no kernel rewrites.

papers.title: Matching Architecture to Workload: Comparing RISC-V Parallel Accelerators for Energy-Efficient Embedded Computing
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25947v1

summary.background:
- Embedded computing: processors built into everyday devices, where power use and chip area matter as much as speed.
- Multicore: several processing cores working in parallel on one chip.
- Vector processing: one instruction operates on a whole row of numbers at once, which suits regular, repetitive math.
- Streaming access: the hardware fetches data in predictable sequences ahead of time, so the processor waits less for memory.
- RISC-V: an open, free instruction set that anyone can build chips around.
- PULP, Snitch, Spatz: three open-source RISC-V accelerator designs, each representing one of the execution models above.
- 12 nm: a chip manufacturing process size, used here so the three designs are compared on equal footing.
- Energy efficiency: how much useful work is done per unit of energy consumed.
summary.one_liner: A controlled comparison, all in 12 nm technology on a common benchmark suite, of three RISC-V parallel accelerator designs (PULP scalar multicore, Snitch streaming multicore, Spatz vector) for energy-efficient embedded workloads.
summary.plain: Small chips inside devices like sensors and wearables often need to do heavy number crunching while using very little power. This paper compares three different ways of organizing the processing cores on such chips, using open-source designs built on the same manufacturing technology and tested on the same set of benchmark programs. The authors find that no single design wins everywhere: one is best for regular, number-heavy tasks, another for tasks with little parallel work, and a third for irregular, control-heavy tasks.
summary.why: Choosing the right processor design for a given job can change both speed and battery use considerably, so these measured trade-offs are useful for anyone designing embedded hardware. The text reports peak gains but does not give the full benchmark breakdown, so the headline numbers should be read as best cases rather than typical results.

papers.abstract: Embedded computing demands high performance and energy efficiency across workloads with widely different computational characteristics. Choosing the most suitable execution model therefore requires a quantitative understanding of how each model maps to different workload classes. In this paper, we compare three execution models for energy-efficient embedded computing: scalar multicore, stream ing multicore, and vector processing. We use three open-source RISC-V accelerators as representative implementations: the PULP Cluster, the Snitch Cluster, and Spatz, respectively. Their open-source hardware and software stacks enable a controlled comparison based on implementations in the same 12 nm technology and a common benchmark suite. Our results reveal that no single execution model performs best across all workload classes. Spatz delivers the greatest benefits for regular and highly vectorizable compute-intensive applications, achieving up to 4.29x higher performance and 5.17x greater energy efficiency than the other architectures. However, its effectiveness strongly depends on the availability of data-level parallelism and regular computation and memory-access patterns, making it the most sensitive to workload characteristics. The Snitch Cluster performs particularly well on applications with limited parallelism and streamable memory-access patterns, providing up to 5.53x higher performance and 1.45x greater energy efficiency. Conversely, the PULP Cluster is most effective on irregular and control-dominated applications, achieving improvements of up to 5.66x in performance and 2.80x in energy efficiency. Compared with Spatz, however, the greater flexibility offered by PULP and Snitch comes at a non-negligible cost in terms of both area and power.

papers.title: From Seed to BLOOM: Autonomously Growing a Better Out-of-Order Core
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26517v1

summary.background:
- Processor core: the central computing block of a CPU that executes instructions.
- Out-of-order superscalar: a design that runs several instructions at once and reorders them to keep hardware busy.
- BOOM: the Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine, an open-source processor design written in hardware description code.
- RTL (register-transfer level): the code that describes what hardware does each clock cycle.
- Synthesis and ASIC: converting that code into a physical chip layout; the reports give area and critical-path (maximum clock speed) estimates.
- IPC (instructions per cycle): a measure of how much work a core completes per clock tick.
- SkyWater 130nm: an older, open chip manufacturing process used for the evaluation.
- SPEC CPU2017: a standard benchmark suite of real programs; wall-clock time combines IPC and clock frequency.
- LLM agent: a language model that plans and carries out multi-step tasks with tools.
summary.one_liner: MiracleGro is an LLM-agent system that autonomously analyzes cycle-level RTL behavior and synthesis results of the open-source BOOM out-of-order RISC-V core, then implements architectural changes that the paper reports as improving IPC, clock frequency and wall-clock time on SPEC CPU2017 in SkyWater 130nm.
summary.plain: Designing a faster computer chip takes teams of experts many months of work. This paper describes an AI system that tries to do much of that work on its own: it looks at how a chip design behaves cycle by cycle and at synthesis reports, spots slow spots, and writes new hardware code to fix them. The authors report that the resulting modified processor ran a large standard benchmark suite about 2.34 times faster in wall-clock time than the original human-designed version.
summary.why: It is a concrete attempt to use frontier AI models for hardware design, a task that usually needs large engineering teams, so small research groups could potentially benefit. The text does not show how general the gains are beyond this one core, one process technology and one benchmark suite, so the wider impact remains to be seen.

papers.abstract: Improving microprocessor performance while meeting ASIC implementation constraints like area and frequency is a complex and labor-intensive task that requires expertise across computer architecture, hardware design, and performance analysis and profiling. While large teams in industry can afford the engineering resources to target this problem across performance modeling, RTL design, and ASIC implementations, small teams of researchers and engineers cannot take on this huge engineering burden while keeping up with the pace of advancement in processor microarchitecture. Recent advancements in large language model (LLM) agents present a promising substrate to accelerate this traditionally human-intensive process. In this work, we build and evaluate MiracleGro, an agentic AI-based system that, without human intervention, analyzes cycle-level RTL behavior and synthesis results, identifies performance bottlenecks, and translates architectural ideas into RTL implementation in a leading open-source out-of-order superscalar application core, the Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine (BOOM). Taking into account cycle-exact performance, area, and critical path, MiracleGro automatically produces improved BOOM designs that drastically increase the human-optimized BOOM's performance on substantial workload suites such as SPEC CPU2017 with full reference inputs. MiracleGro achieves an 85% IPC speedup and a frequency improvement of 27% in SkyWater 130nm, resulting in a 2.34x wall-clock time speedup on the full SPEC CPU2017 intspeed benchmarks (30 trillion instructions). This result demonstrates the enormous opportunity to harness frontier models to improve state-of-the-art RTL-driven platforms for implementation-grounded microarchitecture research across hardware designs.

papers.title: TechReport: Implementing CHERI in gem5
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24460v1

summary.background:
- Memory safety: preventing programs from accessing memory beyond what they are meant to use, a common source of security flaws.
- CHERI (Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions): a processor extension where pointers carry hardware-checked permissions and bounds, called capabilities.
- ISA (instruction set architecture): the set of basic instructions a processor understands; simulators model these.
- gem5: an open-source simulator that models processor hardware in detail, used for architecture research.
- Microarchitecture: the internal organization of a processor (pipelines, caches) that determines speed.
- CheriBSD: a version of the FreeBSD operating system adapted for CHERI.
summary.one_liner: The paper presents gem5-CHERI, an extension of the gem5 microarchitectural simulator that adds CHERI capability-based memory protection and can boot the CheriBSD operating system and run custom workloads, with the code released open-source on GitHub.
summary.plain: Software often fails because programs read or write memory they should not touch, and many security bugs come from this. The authors describe CHERI, a hardware design approach that tags memory references with built-in limits, and they add it to gem5, a widely used computer simulator, so designers can test how such protection behaves in detailed models of processors. The text says the simulator can boot a CHERI-enabled version of FreeBSD (CheriBSD) and run custom programs.
summary.why: Before this, there was no detailed simulator for CHERI designs, so the speed cost of this protection was described as understudied. A tool like this could let researchers measure that cost and explore design choices, though the text does not report any performance results.

papers.abstract: Despite countless mitigation efforts, memory safety issues still prevail. The recently discovered security issues in PHP underline this fact. One of the most promising approaches to solving this problem is the concept of Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions (CHERI). There is a well-developed ecosystem of ISA simulators, compilers, operating systems, and hardware designs that support CHERI. However, the lack of a simulator modeling microarchitectural detail hinders efficient and fast design space exploration for CHERI-enhanced designs means the performance impact of CHERI remains understudied. Therefore, we present gem5-CHERI: a CHERI-enhanced adaptation of the gem5 simulator that can boot the CheriBSD operating system and run custom workloads. The simulator is available open-source on GitHub.

papers.title: Polymorph: Operating System Kernel Optimization Through Artificial Intelligence
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23644v1

summary.background:
- Kernel: the core software that manages a computer's hardware, memory and running programs.
- Page cache: memory the system uses to keep recently read disk data ready, so it doesn't have to be re-read from disk.
- LRU (least recently used): a simple rule that evicts the data that has gone unused the longest.
- Process scheduler: the part of the OS that decides which program gets the processor next.
- eBPF and sched_ext: mechanisms that let user-written code extend parts of the Linux kernel safely without recompiling it.
- Tokens: units of text processed by an AI model; the paper uses token counts as a proxy for AI cost.
- Throughput: how much work gets completed per unit time.
summary.one_liner: Polymorph uses an AI agent to write a generalized eBPF/sched_ext policy for the Linux page cache and process scheduler once, then lets a user-space tuner adjust its parameters online without an LLM in the loop.
summary.plain: Modern operating systems like Linux let developers plug in custom rules for how the computer manages memory caching and deciding which task runs next, without rebuilding the whole system. This paper asks whether an AI system can write those rules automatically. The authors report that their approach, Polymorph, gives a modest throughput gain for the page cache on data it was not trained on, and a larger speedup for the scheduler across six test workloads, at a lower AI cost than prior search methods.
summary.why: Choosing the right kernel policy for each workload is a practical problem for anyone running large servers, so automating it could matter. The text reports specific numbers (8.4% on unseen data, 2.75x versus 2.27x for the best fixed scheduler policy), but these come from the authors' own evaluation, and I cannot judge from the abstract alone how broadly they hold.

papers.abstract: While popular operating systems such as Linux and Windows were originally designed as monolithic kernels, an increasing number of kernel subsystems have become extensible using eBPF. Users can now define custom policies for essential kernel mechanisms, such as the process scheduler, page cache, and network stack, without recompiling the kernel. These mechanisms give developers significant freedom to fit the kernel to their applications' workloads, but the question of which policy to deploy remains open. We study how to use agentic AI to automate kernel policy development, selection, and deployment, focusing on the page cache and the process scheduler as two representative subsystems. We show that existing approaches fall short: evolutionary and agentic search runs offline, is relatively expensive, and often fails to generalize to online workloads, while online knob tuners are encumbered by the knobs' lack of expressivity. In contrast, we propose Polymorph, which learns online: an AI agent writes a generalized, granular policy once, and a user mode tuner adjusts its parameters during runtime, with no LLM in the loop. For the page cache, Polymorph improves throughput over Linux's LRU by 8.4% on unseen data, nearly twice the gain of the best existing policy, while adapting to workload changes at runtime and costing only 16M tokens once, versus 125-240M tokens per workload for agentic offline search. For the process scheduler, it improves on Linux's default by 2.75x across six workloads, versus 2.27x for the best fixed sched_ext policy.

papers.title: On Traffic Characterization in Time-Sensitive Networking and Deterministic Networking
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22744v1

summary.background:
- Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN): IEEE Ethernet extensions that give certain streams guaranteed low, predictable delay.
- Deterministic Networking (DetNet): an IETF effort with similar goals for routed networks.
- TSpec (traffic specification): the short description of a stream's burst pattern, here as (time window, max packet size, max packet count).
- Traffic characterization: a rule that bounds how much data a stream can send over any time span.
- Token-bucket model: a standard way to bound bursts, where a bucket fills at a steady rate up to a maximum size.
- Backlog and delay bounds: worst-case amount of queued data and worst-case waiting time in a device.
- Aggregate: several flows combined and treated as one stream.
- Bounded-delay system: a device guaranteed to forward data within some maximum delay.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives an equivalent traffic characterization for the TSN TSpec, derives how a flow's TSpec changes after passing through a bounded-delay system, characterizes aggregates of TSN flows, and links TSN traffic descriptions to token-bucket bounds for backlog and delay.
summary.plain: Time-sensitive networks carry audio, video and control data with strict timing, and each stream is described by a short set of numbers: a time window, a maximum packet size, and a maximum packet count within that window. This paper asks what happens to that description after a stream passes through a network device, how to describe several streams merged together, and how the description can be used to bound queue lengths and delays. The authors report a set of results that together form a calculus for these descriptions, but the text provided does not include their proofs or any measured performance.
summary.why: Engineers building TSN and DetNet networks need guaranteed worst-case delays for industrial, automotive and audio-video systems, so a sound way to track traffic descriptions through devices and aggregates matters for those guarantees. The work is theoretical, and the text does not show how it performs in practice or in any deployed system.

papers.abstract: The traffic of an audio/video stream in IEEE Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) or an asynchronous traffic flow in IETF Deterministic Networking is specified by three parameters: an observation time interval, a maximum packet size, and a maximum number of packets in the interval. This traffic specification (TSpec) triggers three fundamental questions for TSN and DetNet: (1) if and how the traffic of a flow can be specified by these parameters after it traverses a system, (2) how to specify the traffic of a flow aggregate using the three parameters, and (3) how to use it in performance guarantee analysis. Among them, the literature has focused on (3), leaving the other two little investigated and largely open. This paper is intended to bridge the gap. Specifically, we introduce an equivalent traffic characterization for TSN TSpec, which is simple in representation and simplifies analytical development. Based on this result, we establish an output characterization property for (1) and show that the output of a TSN flow traversing a bounded-delay system can be characterized by the TSN TSpec with updated parameters. For (2) we study the superposition of TSN flows and derive TSN traffic characterizations for the aggregate of multiple TSN flows. For (3), based on a relationship between the TSN traffic characterization and the well-known token-bucket traffic characterization, backlog and delay bounds are derived. Together, these results form a calculus for TSN traffic characterization.

papers.title: Manufacturing Differential Sparsity: Planner-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient World Model Planning
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22483v1

summary.background:
- World model: a learned model that predicts how the environment will change in response to actions.
- JEPA-style latent world model: a predictor that works in a compressed internal representation ("latent" space) rather than raw pixels.
- Model predictive control (MPC): choosing actions by repeatedly simulating many candidate action sequences with the model and picking the best one.
- Quantization: storing numbers with fewer bits to save computation and memory.
- Bit-level sparsity: many bits in the numbers are zero, and hardware can skip work on those zero bits.
- Differential sparsity: sparsity that appears in the difference between a value and a nearby reference value, so similar inputs yield mostly-zero differences.
- Dense accelerator: a chip that performs every multiply without skipping zeros.
- Co-design: designing the algorithm and the hardware together so each shapes the other.
summary.one_liner: A planner-hardware co-design that makes sampling-based model predictive control over JEPA-style latent world models cheaper by having the planner group candidate action sequences around shared roots, which increases differential bit-level sparsity that a bit-sparse accelerator then exploits.
summary.plain: Robots and other embodied agents often imagine possible futures with a learned "world model" before choosing an action, but this imagining is so repetitive that one planning step can take tens of seconds even on a high-end GPU. The paper's approach is to have the planning step itself group similar candidate action sequences together, so the calculations for neighbouring candidates overlap and can be skipped or reused in custom hardware. The authors report that on three such models, their combined planner and chip design runs 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and 1.22-1.58x faster than a prior bit-sparse design, using 16-36% less energy than that prior design, with the same chip area.
summary.why: Real-time planning is a practical bottleneck for robots that must reason about new goals, and this work shows that software and hardware can be designed together rather than separately. Whether the speedups hold beyond the three tested models and on real robots is not shown in the text.

papers.abstract: JEPA-style latent world models let embodied agents plan toward new goals with model predictive control, but they are still too slow for real-life embodied control: sampling-based MPC repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, and even on high-end GPUs one planning step can take tens of seconds. We observe substantial latent locality in this repeated-inference workload: the predictor maps close actions to close latents, and inside a quantized predictor this closeness takes a form that hardware can exploit, differential bit-level sparsity. Unlike an input stream, whose temporal similarity is given, a planner itself decides which candidates it evaluates together, so the planner can choose its own references and, with reference forest sampling, manufacture more sparsity: it couples the sampled action sequences of each group to a shared root, with competitive planning quality. We build the accelerator on the insights of the rich line of bit-level sparsity accelerators and design it and the planner tightly coupled as a single co-design: the planner increases sparsity and exposes structure for hardware scheduling, and the bit-exact hardware effectively uses the sparsity that the planner creates. On three JEPA world models, our co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and uses 38-52% less energy, and it is 1.22-1.58x faster than prior bit-sparse design and uses 16-36% less energy, with the same area. To our knowledge, our planner is the first planner that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity across its candidates and exposes its structure for hardware scheduling, and our co-design is the first algorithm-hardware co-design for JEPA-style world-model planning.

papers.title: One Mean Can't Rule Them All
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20618v1

summary.background:
- A "mean" is a single number that summarizes a set of values; common types include the arithmetic mean (ordinary average), geometric mean (multiplies values and takes a root, suited to ratios), and harmonic mean (suited to rates).
- A "benchmark" is a standard test program used to measure how fast a computer runs typical work.
- Performance summaries across many benchmarks often combine speedup ratios, and the choice of mean can change which system appears better.
- The article is a short position-style piece; only its introduction is available here.
summary.one_liner: A short article proposing a systematic way to pick the right mean (such as arithmetic, geometric, or harmonic) for summarizing computer performance results.
summary.plain: Computer researchers often disagree about how to boil many benchmark timings or speed measurements into a single average. This paper, based only on its opening summary, sets out a systematic method for choosing which kind of average to use, with the stated aim of settling the question. The text provided is only the abstract-level introduction, so the specific method and its results are not described here.
summary.why: Choosing the wrong average can make one computer system look faster than another when the comparison is actually misleading, so the question affects how performance claims are judged. The text does not show how widely the proposed approach has been adopted or tested, so its practical impact is uncertain.

papers.abstract: There has been extensive debate on how to summarize performance results, especially within the computer architecture community. This article presents a systematic approach to choosing the correct mean, aiming to answer this question for all computer scientists once and for all.

papers.title: Top-Level Operational Equilibrium: When is the response of a distributed system predictable from its own telemetry?
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20780v1

summary.background:
- Distributed system: many servers or services working together, often across edge devices and cloud data centres.
- Telemetry: the measurements a system already logs, such as queue lengths and throughput.
- Equilibrium / stationarity: statistical behaviour that does not drift over time.
- Time-reversibility: the statistics look the same when the time sequence is run backwards.
- Sufficient statistic: a summary that keeps all the information needed about a quantity.
- Fluctuation-response identity: a physics-style result relating how a system's random ups and downs predict how it reacts to a small push.
- Queueing terms: a stage is a server with a waiting line; throughput is how much work finishes per unit time; work in progress is the total items inside the system.
- Hysteretic autoscaler: a scaling rule that changes behaviour depending on recent history, so it does not respond the same way twice.
summary.one_liner: The paper defines top-level operational equilibrium (TLOE) for running distributed systems, with stationarity, sufficiency and time-reversibility conditions, and uses a fluctuation-response identity to predict small responses to control changes from passive telemetry, tested only on reference models.
summary.plain: Cloud and edge systems are constantly rescaled and rerouted, and each change assumes the system will respond in a predictable way. The paper asks when that response can be read from the telemetry operators already collect, and gives a set of conditions under which it can. On simple reference models, the authors report that the prediction works for load changes in one class of queueing chain, fails for capacity changes at the first or last stage, and needs specific window lengths of data.
summary.why: Operators adjust systems without a reliable way to know whether the system's reaction is predictable, so a telemetry-based test would be useful if it holds up. The results are only on reference models and simulated data, and real telemetry is explicitly left to future work, so practical value is not yet shown.

papers.abstract: Distributed systems deployed across the edge-cloud continuum are adapted continuously: scaled, re-routed, given more or less capacity. Each adaptation rests on an expectation of how the system will respond, yet operators cannot tell from the telemetry they already collect whether that response is predictable. We define top-level operational equilibrium (TLOE), a notion of equilibrium for a running system, stated relative to the controls its operator declares. TLOE has three conditions: stationarity with time-scale separation, sufficiency of a top-level aggregate for the controls, and time-reversibility of that aggregate. We prove that an aggregate satisfying the last two exists if and only if the minimal sufficient statistic of the controls is time-reversible, so the coarsest admissible aggregate is derived rather than chosen. Under the first two conditions, the response to a small control change follows from passive telemetry through the steady-state fluctuation-response identity, with a conjugate observable fixed by the type of control: the total work in progress for a change of load, the occupancy of a stage for a change of its capacity. For chains of exponential single-server stages with Poisson input, TLOE holds exactly for load control at every stable throughput, but never for a control on the capacity of the first or last stage. On reference models, a per-stage conjugate overestimates the early response about threefold, blocking between stages breaks both conditions weakly, and a hysteretic autoscaler leaves no admissible aggregate at any reaction time computed. We specify a test for each condition, show that a static sufficiency test with an estimated top-level conjugate has no power, and quantify on simulated telemetry the window lengths the prediction and the reversibility test need. The evidence is on reference models; real telemetry is left to future work.
